title: The Teaching Power of a Double Demonstration
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article describes an unusual coaching technique called the Double Demonstration, in which a leader assigns a task with minimal direction, lets the team member complete it independently, then completes the same task themselves before comparing the two results side by side. The comparison, the author argues, often surfaces exactly what has been holding a team member back in a way that direct instruction never could. The technique requires real confidence from the leader, since it exposes their own approach to comparison and critique. The piece closes by framing the willingness to be compared as itself a form of leadership humility that opens a path forward for others.
points: The Double Demonstration technique has a leader and a team member independently complete the same task, then compare results.
The side-by-side comparison often reveals exactly what's been limiting a team member's performance.
This method requires real self-confidence from the leader, since it exposes their own work to direct comparison.
The willingness to be compared and critiqued alongside a team member is framed as an act of leadership humility.
quotes: Leaders intuitively know that giving team members too much direction or process can stunt their development.
This is when leaders ask a team member to execute on a task or assignment without much direction and to keep their end product or solution to themselves for a time.
This Double Demonstration often turbo-charges learning in a way nothing else can.
It is not uncommon for a team member to finally understand what has been holding them back in creating better outcomes.
By definition, high performance is a demonstration of skill.
Exposing the assumptions, choices, and strategies of high performance is a lens into learning like none other.
